items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/28/26
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
We’re easing towards the end of the Thanksgiving break, and closer and closer to a lockout-shaped break imposed by MLB owners. We’ll see if the league has one last offseason frenzy in it before things go dark. We saw a flurry ahead of Thanksgiving last week, and with the CBA set to expire on December 1st, it’s fair to wonder if we’ll get another surge to the finish line. Such a surge may have begun last night, the Blue Jays firing the hot stove up again last night to ink Jazz Chisholm Jr. to a one-year deal worth $20 million.

That marks the official end of Chisholm’s Yankee tenure, though it had been assumed for weeks that he’d be departing. The Yankees themselves have been quiet the last few days, though they seem poised to potentially make a major move. The Adrian Morejon sweepstakes appear ready to resolve, and ideally we’ll get a clearer picture of the shape of the Yankees’ offseason plan before the lights go off.

1. At this point, what do you think Adrian Morejon’s eventual contract will end up at? In excess of $100MM?

2. Weere you surprised to see Jazz Chisholm Jr. take what’s essentially a pillow contract?

items.title: Yankees news: Black Friday Shopping
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
MLB Trade Rumors | Mark Polishuk: Ever since the trade deadline, the Yankees have made it very clear that they have wanted to add to their catching contingent, looking for a right-handed bat to go alongside the lefty-swinging Austin Wells. With San Diego looking to clear a path to playing time for top prospect Ethan Salas, two names that the Yankees have been looking into are Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin. While both are right-handed hitters, their profiles are remarkably different: Fermin would give the Yankees one of the best defensive tandems in the game, and Campusano would provide some power behind the dish the team has desperately needed in recent years. For what it’s worth, not only have the two teams made some high-profile moves in recent years, the situation very much mimics the 2023-2024 winter: the Padres need rotation help, the Yankees have an excess of starters, and the Padres have exactly what the Yankees need.

ESPN | Jorge Castillo: As Andrew detailed for us yesterday, former Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. agreed to a one-year contract with the Toronto Blue Jays that contains both a player and a team option for 2028 and which guarantees him $34.5 million. The move brings to a close a dramatic Yankees career for the 28-year-old infielder, which saw him provide a spark to a scuffling 2024 squad and become a key contributor at the hot corner as the team went to the World Series for the first time since 2009, fill a critical role in the middle of the order in 2025, before scuffling in his contract year while courting controversy on and off the field.

MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: As Friday came to a close, we learned that another multi-year Yankee who hit free agency would not be returning in 2027. Steady long man Ryan Yarbrough is signing with the Cubs, per Robert Murray of FanSided (who also broke the Chisholm news). The Yankees’ decision to sign Brent Suter essentially rendered Yarbrough’s possible future with the team redundant, as Suter has a similar profile and better stuff. Between Suter, Brent Headrick, and Tim Hill, the bullpen was getting fairly left-handed regardless.

The Athletic | Jayson Stark: (subscription required) Following Tarik Skubal’s record-breaking nine-year, $450 million megacontract with the New York Mets, Jayson Stark of decided to rank the best and worst free agent contracts ( extensions) signed by pitchers over the years. Perhaps unsurprisingly, two of the five best belong to the Yankees: CC Sabathia, who led the Yankees to the 2009 World Series in the first year of his deal, and Gerrit Cole, who has won one Cy Young and finished as the runner-up one other time over the first seven years of his deal.

items.title: Blue Jays sign former Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr.
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
The moment that the Yankees decided to pass on giving free agent second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. the one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer, his fate was all but set in stone. It was almost the exact same situation as a couple years ago with Gleyber Torres, who also had a perfectly reasonable case to at least be given the option of returning to New York on a one-year, make-good QO. But for one reason or another, the Yankees’ front office came to the conclusion that they were at the end of the rope with Gleyber, and the same has come to fruition with Jazz.

Chisholm found a new home today and it’s still in the AL East: Toronto. The Blue Jays came to terms with the second baseman on a one-year, $18.5 million deal for 2027 ($12.5 million in salary plus a $6 million signing bonus) that also has a funky option for 2028. It’s a $16 million player option, but if Jazz declines it, then the Jays still have a chance to bring him back on a pretty big $40 million club option. If they decline that and give him a $1.5 million buyout, then he’s a free agent next offseason as well. So if Jazz has a great year for Toronto and thinks he could beat $16 million, then Toronto still has a chance to bring him back on a hefty price tag, albeit hefty for just one year. The bottom line is that he’s locked into $34.5 million even if he repeats his up-and-down 2026 or regresses.

Chisholm’s 2026 campaign with the Yankees was a bit of a mess and we don’t need to go back into it in great detail. It was a disappointing walk year and we subsequently gave it a poor grade in our report card series. In a vaccum, Jazz was still productive in 2026 (a 98 wRC+ and good defense per FanGraphs still gave him 3.5 fWAR), but his slugging tumbled from a 30/30 guy in 2025 with .491 SLG to 19 homers with a .399 SLG. That looks bad when mixed in with his worst strikeout rates since 2023, and his highest in any season of at least 400 plate apperances. Still, Chisholm stole 41 bases as well and it’s not hard to envision a scenario where he becomes a pest again next year. It’s a reasonable gamble from Toronto’s perspective, and even if you’re tired with Jazz’s bit, the prospect of “Anthony Volpe, 2027 Yankees second baseman” isn’t particularly enthralling, either.

The high-variance outcomes at the plate seem to have alarmed the Yankees, and they probably also weren’t entirely thrilled by other incidents surrounding him. Your mileage may vary on them, but I know that I was personally more annoyed by unapologetic postgame quote after a brutal postseason error than the lollipop incident, which was just goofy. Jazz is Jazz. The Blue Jays’ fans will find this to be true as well. Now, will he come closer to the superlative 2025 version or the chaotic 2026 version?

We’ll learn the answer from a distance — but not too much of a distance. I’ve already made my guess.

items.title: Percy Jackson, the Helm of Hades, and Annabeth Chase’s Yankees hat
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
Earlier today, the third and fourth episodes of Percy Jackson and the Olympians season three premiered on Disney+. Adapted from the Rick Riordan books of the same name, the series centers on the titular son of Poseidon as he and his friends grappled with the gods and monsters of the ancient Greeks and Romans, alive and well and living in North America. Two years ago, in the aftermath of the season one finale (and our Top 100 Yankees series here at Pinstripe Alley), I dove into Yankees history, asking the rather amusing question, “Which legendary Yankees figures were secretly the gods of Mt. Olympus?”

As the new season of the television show approached, I found myself thinking about another place where Percy Jackson and baseball intersect: Annabeth Chase’s Yankees hat. A gift from her mother, the goddess Athena, the Yankees hat is more than a simple baseball cap, also functioning as a magical item that turns the wearer invisible. For those who know Greek mythology, it is a clear reference to the Helm of Hades (also known variously as the Helm of Darkness, the Cap of Hades, and the Cap of Invisibility), a magical item normally associated with the God of the Underworld but which others use sporadically throughout Greek mythological history.

Within the Percy Jackson universe, items and places from Greek myths are reimagined all the time: Mt. Olympus is in the Empire State Building, Charon the ferryman is an elevator operator, and Apollo’s sun chariot is a sports car. And so I began to wonder, why did the author decide to make a magical item inspired by the Helm (but which is itself not the helm — that specific item appears elsewhere in the story) out of a Yankees hat?

To answer that question, we first need to dive a bit into the mythical helm. While it’s hard to find an ancient depiction of it, here’s how Renaissance and Enlightenment era artists tended to depict it, as seen through this statue of Perseus holding the head of Medusa:

Sure, this doesn’t help us understand what the ancient one looked like (that’s a bit harder to determine), but it does show us that… well, it’s not some big special thing, just a normal everyday item that is imbued with magical properties. This, in fact, reflects most things in mythology: modern depictions of Cerberus, the guard dog of Hades, depict him as a big, scary monster, but in antiquity he was just a simple dog that happened to have three heads; see, for example, this statue group of Hades, Persephone, and Cerberus from the first century BCE:

With that in mind, it’s clear that, for a modern day invisibility cap, Riordan was looking not for something extraordinary and noticeable, but rather something incredibly mundane. And in the United States in the 21st century, what headwear is more mundane than a baseball cap? I mean, baseball caps with the logos of basketball, football, hockey, and soccer teams are everywhere. Colleges and high schools plaster their school logo on them. Even the US military and veterans’ organizations employ baseball caps, both as part of certain uniforms and as non-uniform gear. The baseball cap has spread well beyond its original use on the diamond, and has become one of, if not arguably the, American fashion accessory.

So it makes sense why Riordan would make the modern-day cap of invisibility out of a baseball cap. But why, specifically, a Yankees hat? It could simply be narrative convenience — the Percy Jackson series centers on New York, and when people think of baseball hats in New York City, they tend to think of Yankee hats (apologies to any Mets fans reading this, but it’s true). Narrative convenience, though, is not in my mind a sufficient answer, even if it hints at the real answer: the author immediately jumps from baseball cap to Yankee hat because, ultimately, the Yankee hat is the default baseball cap not just in New York, but within public consciousness. Check out, for example, the Wikipedia page for “baseball cap;” at the time of writing, the top image on the page, normally designed to give the reader an understanding of the topic, is a Yankee hat. And so, when trying to create the most mundane, unexciting, run-of-the-mill modern hat? Well, in truth, there’s only one option.

items.title: Yankee Birthday of the Day: Bullet Joe Bush
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
A good chunk of the heroes from Yankees history are one-team players who spent their entire careers in the Bronx. I’m talking Lou Gehrig, Joe DiMaggio, and Mickey Mantle to modern ones like Derek Jeter and Aaron Judge.

However, it’s somewhat well known that the first couple decades in franchise history weren’t very successful. When the Yankees did finally reach the mountain top in 1923, the roster — including Babe Ruth — had a lot of key players who had notable runs elsewhere that had been acquired through trades.

One of that list includes Bullet Joe Bush, who would be celebrating a birthday today.

Leslie Ambrose “Bullet Joe” Bush November 27, 1892 (Ehime, MN) November 1, 1974 (Fort Lauderdale, FL) 1922-24

Bush was born in Minnesota in 1892, one of seven children. He was dubbed “Joe” as a child, although the Bullet part of his nickname wasn’t added until his baseball career, as you might expect. As a child, Bush was said to practice his pitching by throwing “rotten apples through a crescent-shaped hole of a neighboring outhouse.”

He began playing more organized baseball for the Brainerd, MN town team when he was 13 years old. Originally, Bush played third base. However, he was converted to a pitcher after the team captain noticed the speed at which his throws came in at. That’s when he truly began to get noticed, and a Montana-based minor league team eventually signed him when Bush was 18.

In Montana, Bush’s manager was Cliff Blankenship, who had been credited for discovering Hall of Fame pitcher Walter Johnson. Blankenship mentored Bush before recommending him to Philadelphia Athletics’ manager Connie Mack. The A’s legend took his advice, and Bush was soon making his MLB debut as a 19-year old in August 1912.

In 1913, A’s ace Jack Coombs missed most of the season with an illness, which led to Bush getting a more prominent role for the team. His numbers on the whole weren’t spectacular, but he went 15-6 for Philadelphia as they won the AL pennant. In the World Series, Bush was entrusted to start Game 3, and allowed just two runs (one earned) in a complete game victory over the Giants. The series was tied going into Game 3 and Philadelphia rode that win to take the series in five.

After that season, Bush became a fixture in the A’s rotation. It took until 1916 for his rate stats like ERA to become genuinely good, but he did help Philadelphia make it back to the World Series in 1914, although they were swept by the Braves.

However, as Bush began to become an excellent pitcher, the A’s team began to become way less than excellent. With the introduction of the rebel Federal League, Mack began to sell away players from that 1913 World Series-winning team rather than get into bidding wars, including Home Run Baker to the Yankees. It was hardly all his fault, but Bush ended up suffering a league-leading 24 losses in 1916.

Eventually, Bush became part of the A’s sell-off and he was sent to the Red Sox in December 1917. In Boston, Bush immediately turned in one his best seasons to date in 1918, helping the Red Sox to the World Series. Boston ended up beating the Cubs in six games in the series. Bush lost his only start in Game 2, but he came out of the bullpen in Game 4. A still-pitching Babe Ruth was nursing a one-run lead going into the ninth but allowed the first two runners to reach. Bush came in and got a bunt force out at third and a double play to seal a 3-2 win. That gave Boston a crucial 3-1 lead in the series.

An arm injury forced Bush to miss almost all of the 1919 season, but he came back in 1920 armed with a new weapon. During his return from injury, Bush stumbled across the forkball, which he is credited with inventing. While he was only okay in 1920, by 1921 he had mastered the pitch and was back to his best.

However once again, financial concerns soon led to the breakup of a World Series-winning team Bush was on. Red Sox owner Harry Frazee began selling off players from that 1918 team. Many of those deals saw Red Sox stars going to the Yankees, most notably Ruth. Bush eventually became part of that list as he, fellow pitcher Sad Sam Jones, and shortstop Everett Scott were traded to New York in December 1921.

Once again though, Bush joined a team on the brink of success. Thanks in part to Bush’s 26 wins, the Yankees won the AL pennant in 1922, although they fell to the Giants in the World Series. However the following year, Bush pitched a team-high 275.2 innings, helping the team back to the World Series. This time they emerged victorious, besting the Giants in six games. Bush himself got dinged with a loss in Game 1 despite allowing only one run in 6.2 innings out of the bullpen. In Game 5, he again came up big in the Fall Classic, allowing just one run in a complete game, giving the Yankees a 3-2 lead in the series. They clinched the franchise’s first championship the following day.

Bush had a down season in 1924 as the Yankees failed to make it back to the World Series. The team opted to trade him to the St. Louis Browns for fellow pitcher Urban Shocker. Bush became a bit of a journeyman after that, playing for several teams before ending his MLB career back with the A’s in 1928.

After a couple more years playing in the minors, Bush transitioned to coaching and led the Allentown Buffaloes to the Eastern League pennant in 1930. After leaving baseball, Bush held a variety of jobs before retiring to Florida, where he lived until passing away in 1974.

Bullet Joe Bush is one of just two dozen or so players to have won a World Series championship with three different teams. He also came up remarkably big in all of those championships too.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees Potential Free Agent Target: Seiya Suzuki
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The hot stove has combusted into an inferno with less than a week to go before the expiration of the CBA at 11:59 pm ET on December 1st. Tarik Skubal was the first domino to fall, igniting a flurry of subsequent moves that has seen teams guarantee well over $1 billion in a three-day span. The Yankees, meanwhile, prefer to wade in the shallow end of the pool, committing modest outlays for relievers Jonathan Loáisiga, Tim Hill, and Brent Suter after receiving confirmation that closer David Bednar would return on the qualifying offer. There have been only wisps of smoke behind rumors linking them to additions on the position player side, recent comments from Brian Cashman hinting at a level of comfort to run it back with the in-house offense yet again. While corner outfield is certainly not an area of need, Seiya Suzuki represents one of the best available bats in a barren class of free agent hitters.

143 games, 634 PA, .270/.368/.473, 26 HR, 31 doubles, 86 RBI, 131 OPS+, 134 wRC+, 14 DRS, +5 OAA, 4.5 fWAR, 5.1 rWAR

2026 FanGraphs Depths Charts Projections: 149 games, 644 PA, .256/.346/.448, 24 HR, 30 doubles, 82 RBI, 120 wRC+, 2.7 fWAR

At the beginning of the week, my colleague John analyzed Randy Arozarena’s prospective free agent fit. It is actually uncanny how similar the two corner outfielders profile to each other. The pair were born within six months of each other and have generally been well below average with the glove (2026 notwithstanding in Suzuki’s case). They both hit 26 home runs in 2026, sport a 128 wRC+ for their careers, and posted nearly identical triple-slash lines — .270/.368/.473 from Suzuki and .281/.381/.484 from Arozarena. FanGraphs Depth Charts projects nearly identical outcomes for the pair in 2027 — a 120 wRC+ and 30 doubles for each and a rounding error difference in home runs and fWAR. Arozarena will steal you more bags while Suzuki is a slightly surer bet in the field.

Suzuki has been a remarkably consistent threat on offense since coming over from NPB prior to the 2022 season. Not including that debut season where he was limited to 111 games by injury, Suzuki has appeared in at least 130 games, hit at least 20 home runs, walked over ten percent of the time, and posted a wRC+ above 120 in each of the last four seasons. His pitch recognition is impressive, placing him at or above the 90th percentile in walk and chase rates. He does most of his damage against the fastball — particularly those on the inner half that he can pull in the air — but more than holds his own against off-speed pitches like the changeup and splitter.

This season was a both a career year and a weird outlier campaign of sorts. He posted a career high 4.5 fWAR thanks largely in part to his first ever above-average season on defense — he generally is among the league leaders when it comes to the value he produces with his arm strength and accuracy but typically grades out as slightly below average overall until experiencing a massive improvement in his reaction time in 2026. That being said, Suzuki also regressed in key offensive areas. This season saw him lose about three mph in average and max exit velocity and was the first season since his rookie year that he posted a sub-40-percent hard-hit rate and a sub-.400 expected wOBA on contact despite his average bat speed remaining stable. He has also appeared in over 150 games just once in five seasons and you can likely bake in about a month of missed games given his history with knee, neck, and oblique injuries.

I’m not sure how much I buy the improvement with the glove. That a trio of free agent position players in Suzuki, Brandon Lowe, and Luis Arraez posted their first ever solid defensive seasons on the cusp of or well into their thirties says as much about the noise and fickle nature contained within current defensive metrics as it does any tangible improvements in their defensive capabilities. Projections systems unanimously expect each of the three to regress back closer to their career norms going forward, which relegates Suzuki from All-Star level to solid starter level.

It is hard to see the fit on the Yankees roster. Most projections expect Suzuki to sign in the neighborhood of four years and $100 million. New York already has over $80 million committed to their corner outfielders in 2028. They need a starter in center with Cashman noncommittal on Spencer Jones’ grasp on the job. Suzuki has just 133.2 innings of major league experience in left field under his belt, so you would be asking him to effectively learn a new position in the more difficult Yankee Stadium left field while sliding the best defensive left fielder in MLB in Cody Bellinger over to center, where he’s been merely average since 2020. As much as the Yankees would benefit from slotting his power righty bat into the middle of their lineup, they are better saving their likely limited funds for more pressing needs in center and in the infield.

See more potential Yankees free agent targets here.

items.title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Carlos Rodón
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
Of all the pitchers on the Yankees’ roster, Carlos Rodón was the hardest for me to grade. His traditional numbers, a 7-3 record, 2.67 ERA, and 91 strikeouts, look great in the context of playing only half a season. However, he’s paid like an ace, with a $27 million average annual value, just a quarter million less than Max Fried, and only pitched half a season. The metrics tell a story of a pitcher who ground through the year despite finishing with a dazzling ERA. I was on the low end of the Pinstripe Alley staff, personally issuing a B. The staff average ended up giving the veteran an A-minus, or, as I like to think of it in this situation, an “Ace Light.”

16 games (16 GS), 84.1 IP, 2.67 ERA (158 ERA+), 3.44 FIP, 26.8 K%, 11.2 BB%, 1.8 fWAR, 2.2 rWAR, 7–3 record

$27 million salary (six-year, $162 million contract); full no-trade clause; free agent in 2029

Rodón’s 2026 season really got underway in October 2025, when he underwent surgery to remove loose bodies and shave down a bone spur in his left elbow. This caused Rodón to miss spring training and the first six weeks of the 2026 regular season. The team activated Rodón from the 15-day injured list on May 10th to officially start his 2026 season.

As one would expect, Rodón was rusty initially, and his command was off, to the tune of a 16.0 percent walk rate in May. Rodón needed 354 pitches just to record his first 19 innings of work on the season as he worked on his mechanics and tried to find a consistent release point. He looked better in June but was still issuing free passes at a high rate. Pretty much every start seemed to be a grind, resulting in six innings or fewer and around three earned runs. At the end of June, Rodón’s left elbow flared up and landed him on the shelf. This first stint of his season ended with a 4-2 record and 3.30 ERA across 46.1 innings.

It was not until mid-August that Rodón would return. He made three starts over the rest of the month, and his command looked a lot better. From the first stint to the second, his walk rate was cut nearly in half, from 13.4% before the IL stint (26 BB in 194 TBF) to 8.2% after his return (12 BB in 146 TBF).

The old lefty saved his best for last. In September, over his final four starts, Rodón went 3-0 with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP, 28 strikeouts, and just seven walks across 25.1 innings. Opponents hit just .141 off him during this stretch. The cherry on top was the eight scoreless innings he pitched against the Rays on September 22, which ended up being his final appearance of the season. This win gave him number 100 and he collected strikeout number 1,500 for his career. In this second act of the season he went 3-1 with a 1.89 ERA across 38.0 innings. 

Now, if you’re like me, after seeing all that positive, you might be thinking, that’s not the pitcher I remember watching. That could be due to nearly every underlying indicator suggesting Rodón should have been giving up more runs. Over a larger sample, predictive models peg his true performance closer to the mid-3.00s in ERA (3.29 xERA, 3.44 FIP, 3.73 xFIP, and 4.61 botERA).

Rodón also benefited from some favorable batted-ball results in 2026, posting a .220 BABIP that ranked in the 98th percentile and sat roughly 70 points below league average. There was also a big 50-point gap between opponents’ actual .254 wOBA and their .304 xwOBA, suggesting that hitters were not getting the results their contact quality might have warranted. 

To his credit, Rodón kept the ball in the yard this season, allowing just 0.75 HR/9, and that elite mark, especially for a fly ball pitcher, helped his numbers significantly. Rodón lost command at times, contributing to some difficult innings, but he also found ways to limit the damage and keep opponents off the scoreboard. He did not allow more than three runs in any start and yet only registered six quality starts on the year. 

Rodón’s 2026 season had a dash of batted-ball luck, a run down the stretch where he looked like an ace, and underlying peripherals that look more like those of a solid third option. One last little nugget: Rodón was the Yankees’ Roberto Clemente Award nominee for the second straight season, a commendation on his terrific philanthropic efforts through the foundation he runs with his wife, Ashley. Here’s to hoping 2027 brings a year of health and a continuation of outperforming computer projections.

See more of the Yankees Roster Report Card series here.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/27/26
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
Thanksgiving has come and gone, and if you were one of many watching the football games on display you were treated to some instant classics with Bears-Lions and Eagles-Cowboys giving us some wild comebacks and last-second theatrics (Chiefs-Bills came down to the wire too). Setting our sights back on baseball, the sport continues to approach the end of the CBA and the beginning of what looks to be a nasty lockout, with just four days left before it all goes down. The Yankees are in hot pursuit of one big bullpen signing to wrap up their relief corps retooling before that happens, and we’ll be on high alert if they manage to land Adrián Morejón over the weekend before the buzzer sounds.

We’ve got a busy day as we get back into the swing of things, starting with Jonathan giving out a report card to Carlos Rodón for an abbreviated season. Peter considers Seiya Suzuki’s potential fit on the Yankees’ roster with a fairly similar comp to Randy Arozarena, Matt takes us back to the days of the first Yankees championship for Bullet Joe Bush’s birthday, and John has some fun examining the context of the Percy Jackson series’ choice to use a Yankees cap as a magic item.

1. Have we seen the bulk of the signing rush before the lockout occurs, or are we still in for some hectic buying through these last four days?

2. It’s kind of become a more mundane day than its heyday in the 2000s, but are you heading out to shop Black Friday deals today?

items.title: Yankees news: Catcher market is already drying up
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
NY Post | Mark W. Sánchez: The Yankees are open to bringing in a catcher, especially if he’s a good defender behind the plate and hits from the right side. They may need to hurry up, though, because the market might be drying up: Tyler Stephenson returned to the Reds, Gary Sánchez committed his future to the Marlins, and Ryan Jeffers accepted the Twins’ qualifying offer. Sánchez goes through some of the Yanks’ remaining options, including Carson Kelly, Austin Hedges, Kyle Higashioka, and more.

Heavy: Jonathan Loáisiga agreed to sign a two-year deal with the Yankees this week. As it turns out, according to New York Post’s Jon Heyman, the reliever actually turned down a more lucrative offer from the Mets to return to the Bronx.

NY Post | Greg Joyce: With Paul Goldschmidt signing a one-year deal with the Mets, he wraps up a productive two-year stint with the Yankees. The veteran first baseman revealed the reasons why he decided to move in a different direction. “My top concern was not, ‘Hey, how do I go to someplace where I get the most playing time?’ ” Goldschmidt said Wednesday morning. “My concern was going to a team where it felt right … and just have an opportunity to be on a team that has a chance to win and is going for it. Obviously, the Mets are in that.” The former NL MVP will likely platoon with Jared Young at first base in Queens.

MLB.com | Thomas Harrigan: Harrigan takes a look at the Yankees’ bullpen heading into 2027: signings already made, unsigned free agents, and where the unit stands at this moment, a few days until the looming lockout starts on Dec. 1.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Lefty Gomez
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
The history of the Yankees’ franchise is generally one defined by hitters. Starting with Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig, the franchise’s most recognizable stars are almost always position players, carrying forward to the modern day with Aaron Judge.

However, you cannot win 27 World Series title by throwing out just anyone on the mound. There are still plenty of all-time Yankee greats that were pitchers. One of them was Lefty Gomez, a Hall of Famer in his own right.

Vernon Louis “Lefty” Gomez November 26, 1908 (Rodeo, CA) February 17, 1989 (Greenbrae, CA) 1930-42

Gomez was one of a number of Yankees of his era to come from California, as he was born there in 1908. His father was of Spanish-Portuguese descent and was a cowboy on a farm north of San Francisco. The kid later known as “Lefty” grew up riding horses and milking cows.

In baseball, Gomez grew up playing local sandlot games and was pretty quickly identified as a talent. By 14, he was already getting noticed by the Pacific Coast League’s San Francisco Seals, although they passed on the young, still scrawny Gomez at that time. After his high school career ended, the Seals finally agreed to ink Gomez, although the pitcher had to win over his father, who wished for Lefty to go to college to become an engineer.

The Seals farmed out Gomez in 1928, but brought him into the fold for the following season. San Francisco manager Nick Williams was still very skeptical of the still thin and scrawny pitcher, but Gomez eventually broke into the rotation through undeniable performances on the mound. By the end of the season, he was the Seals’ star, leading the league in ERA. The Yankees eventually took notice and signed him in August, but kept him in San Francisco for the rest of the PCL season.

Upon reporting to the Yankees for 1930, the team had similar concerns about his frame. They sent Gomez to a “health farm” during spring training. However, he impressed enough to start the year in the big leagues with the team. However, he struggled during his rookie campaign. Not only was he a rookie, but Gomez had suffered an injury after getting hit in the face with a liner back in spring training. Doctors suspected that botched dental work in the aftermath of that had caused an infection that was still bothering the pitcher. Gomez eventually got all his upper teeth pulled and replaced and eventually got sent down to the minor league St. Paul Saints.

After a year there, Gomez came back up to the Yankees in 1931, albeit put in the bullpen by new manager Joe McCarthy. However once again, Gomez battled his way into the rotation by simply being too good to deny. By the end of the season, Gomez had won 21 games while posting a 2.67 ERA.

Now a full-fledged star of the rotation, Gomez won another 24 games in 1932, although stats like ERA had him a bit below league average for the season. However, his knack for winning got Gomez the start in Game 2 of that year’s Fall Classic, and he delivered. Gomez threw a complete game allowing just two runs, only one of which was earned. The Yankees won the game and the series in a sweep over the Cubs.

Over the years, Gomez became a star for the Yankees as they became baseball’s preeminent dynasty. Gomez helped the Yankees to four more World Series titles over the course of his career, as they won a then-record four consecutive titles from 1936-39. Not only did Gomez win five championships in five trips to the Fall Classic, but he put up a perfect 6-0 record as a pitcher. That’s both a World Series and an MLB postseason record for the most wins by a pitcher without having ever taken a loss.

Individually, Gomez made seven consecutive All-Star teams from 1933-39. His best year came in 1934, when he won a league-leading 26 games, while also besting baseball in stats like ERA en route to the classic pitching Triple Crown (he won another in 1937), as well as modern ones, including 8.4 rWAR.

Gomez also became known as one of the most colorful characters in baseball, getting the nickname “Goofy.” While Yogi Berra has the most notable quotes of anyone in Yankees’ history, Gomez shouldn’t be far behind. Some of his best include replying to a question about whether he would brush back — another thing he was known for — his own mother with a pitch by saying, “You’re damn right I would. She’s a good hitter.”

Once while facing Bob Feller, Gomez — a horrifically bad hitter, even for a pitcher — lit a match. When asked by the umpire, “Do you think that match will help you see Feller’s fast one?” Gomez said, “No, I’m not concerned about that. I just want to make sure he can see me.” While filling out a job application following his retirement, Gomez listed the reason for leaving his prior employment as “Couldn’t get anybody out.”

In 1939, Gomez suffered an arm injury while covering first base, and that would be the beginning of the end for him. The injury began to affect his pitching motion and he was limited to just 263.2 total innings over the course of the 1940-42 seasons. He did pitch well in the middle of those seasons in 1941, but McCarthy somewhat controversially didn’t use him in the World Series victory over the Dodgers.

The injuries eventually caught up to Gomez, and the Yankees released him in January 1943. He signed with the Boston Braves but was released before ever appearing in a game for them. He was picked up by the Washington Senators, and appeared in one game for them, but was released by them too, marking the end of his baseball career.

Gomez eventually found his way into coaching and managed in the Yankees’ minor league system, including helming a team with a young Whitey Ford. He later left coaching and had a sales job with Wilson Sporting Goods. Thanks to his affable nature, he also became a popular dinner speaker and talk show guest. Gomez was voted into the Hall of Fame by the Veterans Committee in 1972. He eventually settled back in his native California, where he resided until passing away in 1989 at age 80.

Lefty Gomez was an undeniably great pitcher. However, it’s debatable whether he would’ve been as well remembered had he not been a member of those great Yankees teams and was putting up those stats for a middling one. However, he was a reason those Yankees’ teams were as good as they were. After all, you can’t win championships with outstanding talent on just one side of the ball.
